method_card.title: Bar Charts, Pie Charts and Stem-and-Leaf Diagrams
method_card.content:
A pie chart represents data as sectors of a circle. The formula for each sector angle is given on the formula sheet: \(\text{angle} = \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}} \times 360\). Always divide by the total frequency, not by the number of categories.

A comparative pie chart uses two circles of different sizes to compare two datasets. The areas of the circles are proportional to the totals, so a dataset with twice the total has a circle with \(\sqrt{2}\) times the radius — not twice the radius. This is a Higher-tier skill.

For a stem-and-leaf diagram, the stem is the leading digit(s) and the leaf is the final digit. Always include a key (e.g. 3 | 7 means 37). A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram places two datasets either side of a shared stem, allowing direct comparison of shape, median and spread.

Bar charts come in several forms: a dual bar chart places two bars side by side for direct comparison. A composite (stacked) bar chart stacks bars to show both the total and the component parts. A percentage bar chart standardises all bars to 100%, removing the effect of different group sizes.

When reading a Venn diagram, the intersection represents items in both categories. P(A ∩ B) is read from the overlapping region; P(A only) excludes the intersection. Count carefully and always check whether the question asks for a count or a probability.
steps: For a pie sector angle, divide the category frequency by the total, then multiply by 360
For a stem-and-leaf diagram, split each value into its stem (leading digit) and leaf (final digit)
Write the key for any stem-and-leaf diagram (e.g. 2 | 4 means 24)
For back-to-back diagrams, read left-side leaves from right to left (they still increase outward from the stem)
For a Venn diagram, identify the intersection, left-only, right-only and outside regions before answering any question
For comparative pie charts (Higher), check whether you are being asked to compare angles or actual frequencies

exam_context.marks: 2–5 marks; sector angle calculations are 2 marks, back-to-back stem-and-leaf comparisons up to 4 marks
exam_context.frequency: Pie chart sector angles and stem-and-leaf reading appear on most papers; Venn diagram intersection questions appear on roughly half of all papers

worked_examples.question: 30 students were asked their favourite subject. 12 chose Maths. What angle is needed for the Maths sector in a pie chart?
The back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram below shows test scores for two classes. Find the median for each class.

steps.label: Step 1 — Read Class A values in order
steps.content: Reading left leaves right-to-left from the stem: 53, 58, 59, 62, 67, 71, 75 — 7 values, median is the 4th: 62

steps.label: Step 2 — Read Class B values in order
steps.content: 51, 54, 60, 66, 68, 73, 77, 79 — 8 values, median is the mean of the 4th and 5th: \(\frac{66 + 68}{2} = 67\)

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Class A median = 62; Class B median = 67. Class B scored higher on average.

worked_examples.question: The Venn diagram below shows 40 students studying History and Geography. How many study neither subject? What is P(History only)?

steps.label: Step 1 — Find History only and Geography only
Step 2 — Find those studying at least one subject
steps.content: \(16 + 10 + 8 = 34\) students study at least one subject.

steps.label: Step 3 — Find neither and the probability
Answer
steps.content: 6 students study neither subject. P(History only) = 2/5.

bronze.display: A survey of 60 people found 15 preferred tea. What angle represents the tea sector in a pie chart?

misconceptions.message: Angle = (15/60) × 360 = 0.25 × 360 = 90°. Divide by the total (60), not the number of categories.

bronze.display: A pie chart sector for 'Cycling' has an angle of 72°. The pie chart represents 100 people in total. How many people chose cycling?

misconceptions.message: Frequency = (72/360) × 100 = 0.2 × 100 = 20. Reverse the sector-angle formula.

What is the largest value in the stem 3 row?

misconceptions.message: Stem 3 with leaf 8 means 38. The leaves are individual digits appended to the stem. The largest leaf in the stem 3 row is 8, giving 38.

bronze.display: The dual bar chart shows sales for two shops in January and February.

misconceptions.message: Read January bars: Shop A = 40, Shop B = 55. Difference = 55 − 40 = 15 units.

bronze.display: A pie chart has four sectors with angles 90°, 120°, 80°, and x°. Find x.
A back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram is drawn for the ages of members in two clubs. Which property can be directly compared from the diagram?
options: The range and median of both datasets simultaneously
The mean of both datasets without any calculation
The exact variance of each dataset
The cumulative frequency of each dataset

misconceptions.message: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf shows the shape, spread (range) and middle value (median) visually for both sets. It does not give the mean directly — that requires calculation.

bronze.display: Total students = 48. How many students do neither?

misconceptions.message: Students in at least one sport: 13 + 7 + 8 = 28. Neither: 48 − 28 = 20.

misconceptions.message: Angle = (9/45) × 360 = 0.2 × 360 = 72°. Divide by the total 45, not by the number of categories.

misconceptions.message: 9 values ordered: 15, 18, 20, 23, 27, 31, 34, 39. The median is the 5th value: 23. Read the leaves in order, not just pick the middle row.

silver.display: The composite bar chart shows online vs in-store sales for two products.

misconceptions.message: Product B total = 45 + 15 = 60. In-store for B = 15. Percentage = (15/60) × 100 = 25%. Do not use Product A's total.

silver.display: Total = 50 students. What is the probability a randomly chosen student owns a cat but not a dog?

misconceptions.message: Cat only = 14 (the right-only region). P(cat only) = 14/50 = 7/25. The denominator is the total 50, not just those owning cats.

silver.display: The percentage bar chart shows grade 4+ pass rates for Year 10 (120 students) and Year 11 (80 students). Year 10: 40%, Year 11: 65%. How many more Year 10 students than Year 11 students achieved grade 4+?

misconceptions.message: Year 10: 40% of 120 = 48. Year 11: 65% of 80 = 52. Difference = 48 − 52 = −4, so Year 11 has 4 more. Never compare percentages when group sizes differ.

misconceptions.message: Sum all three regions: 24 + 28 + 17 = 69. Neither = 80 − 69 = 11.

Key: 5 | 3 means 53 (X); 5 | 4 means 54 (Y)


Find the interquartile range of Dataset X (n = 9).

misconceptions.message: X ordered: 42, 45, 48, 51, 53, 59, 60, 64, 67. n=9 (one less than a multiple of 4 gives integer positions): Q1 = 2nd value = 45, Q3 = 8th value = 64. IQR = 64 − 45 = 19. For the AQA n=9 rule: Q1 at position (9+1)/4=2.5 → mean of 2nd and 3rd = (45+48)/2 = 46.5; Q3 at 3(9+1)/4=7.5 → (60+64)/2 = 62; IQR = 62−46.5 = 15.5. Check which rule your mark scheme uses.
Read Dataset X leaves from right to left (they increase outward from the stem). Values are 42, 45, 48, 51, 53, 59, 60, 64, 67.

gold.display: The composite bar chart shows frequencies for three segments across two groups.

misconceptions.message: Group 1 total = 30 + 25 + 25 = 80. Segment C for Group 1 = 25. Percentage = (25/80) × 100 = 31.25%.

gold.display: Total = 100 outcomes. How many outcomes are in none of the three events?

misconceptions.message: Each pairwise intersection value shown (8, 6, 4) excludes the triple intersection (3). Add all 7 distinct regions before subtracting from the total.

gold.display: The dual bar chart shows monthly sales for two regions. In which month was the difference between the two regions greatest?

misconceptions.message: Differences: Jan=5, Feb=45, Mar=2, Apr=5. February has the greatest difference (80−35=45). Always calculate absolute differences rather than reading visually.
